paras: The Barnwell County race-war scare was an armed mobilization of white residents near Bamberg, South Carolina, in December 1888, who searched the swamps for Black men supposed to have kidnapped and murdered a white farmer, Robert Morris. Morris was found alive and drunk in the woods two days after he disappeared, and no one of either race was reported harmed. Papers across the country first carried the episode as a threatened "war of races" and then retold its ending as a joke.

The first reports came from Charleston on December 18, bundled with dispatches about other shootings between Black and white men in the state, including one at Blackville, also in Barnwell County, where a white man named Luther Dewitt wounded a Black man named as Tyler or Isaac Taylor.

According to a special dispatch to the New York Evening World, Morris's brother, J. M. Morris, and John McMillan had "a difficulty" with some Black men on Monday, December 17, and that night found their house surrounded by Black men making threats against their lives. The men scattered to rouse the neighbors, but Robert Morris never answered the agreed signal. In another version, the brother returned with help to find Robert's coat, with a hole in it, and his gun, but no trace of him. He was believed "captured and murdered by the infuriated negroes," and young men from Bamberg went to the scene.

Over the next day white residents armed themselves; the Sun reported that "the whites are assembling to capture the murderers and the negroes are collecting to resist." A later Columbia dispatch described "the usual armed posse of whites" scouring the swamps for the body "and also to avenge his murder," while the Black residents "became frightened and hid out." On the night of December 19 the searchers found Morris alive in the woods. A Charleston telegram that night called the supposed plot "a delirium tremens vagary."

No arrests, inquest or charges were reported, and a Columbia wire story stated that "no damage has been done to any one of either color." The people of Bamberg, the Sun's correspondent added, went back to their fields "very much incensed."

At first the papers framed the disappearance as a racial threat: the Savannah Morning News headed its item "Evidence that Barnwell Negroes Have Murdered a White Man," and the Sun warned that "a war of races is threatened." The Connecticut Western News reprinted that alarm on December 26, a week after Morris had been found.

After Morris turned up, the tone shifted to ridicule: under the headlines "He Only Had the Jim-Jams" and "A Race War That Fizzled Out," a Columbia correspondent wrote that the drunken Morris party "lynched imaginary niggers for two nights and a day" while neighbors searched for them. A shorter Columbia wire calling it a "ridiculous ending" ran from December 22 in papers from Annapolis to Rock Island, Illinois, where the Argus headed it "It Was Whisky That Was Killed." A weekly news digest printed on December 29 by the Huntsville Gazette and others said the race war had been "inaugurated by the whites" of the county.

The National Leader of Washington aimed its mockery at the white men. It wrote that the "refined" citizens of Barnwell County had "armed themselves, and turned out en masse to hunt for his body, and avenge his death," only to find Morris "dead drunk in the woods."

Accounts of how Morris came to be in the woods differed: the Sun and Tribune said the whole Morris party got drunk and went out armed after imagined Black men, while the Columbia wire said Morris bought a jug of whisky and "took to the woods to enjoy it." The first report of threats at the Morris house came from the Morris side; the Charleston correction dismissed the whole plot as a delusion. The digest dated the discovery December 21, but dispatches written at the time placed it on the night of December 19. The first Charleston wire said Black residents were "collecting to resist," whereas the Columbia account said they hid.

reader.title: Barnwell County race-war scare (1888)
bases: Armed white residents organized to capture and 'avenge' the supposed Black killers of Robert Morris, a threatened lynching that ended without harm when Morris was found alive (A3, A8, A11).

No one was killed: Morris was found alive and the wire reported no damage to anyone of either color (A7, A11); the armed search to avenge a supposed murder was a threat that was never carried out (A8).

Separate Charleston dispatches (A1, A2/A3) and Columbia dispatches (A8, A11) agree that Morris was reported murdered by Black men, that whites armed to search, and that he was found alive and drunk (A6, A7).

accounts.gist: J. M. Morris and John McMillan had a difficulty with Black men, who that night surrounded the house making threats; the men scattered for help, and Robert never answered the signal; his coat with a hole and his gun were found, and he was believed captured and murdered.

accounts.label: Charleston correction
accounts.gist: Morris was found in a drunken delirium, and the supposed plot was a delirium tremens delusion.

accounts.label: Columbia special (Sun, Tribune)
accounts.gist: The Morris family got their Christmas whiskey early; the drunken party went out armed after imagined Black men and got lost for two nights and a day while an armed posse searched the swamps to find and avenge them.

accounts.label: Columbia wire
accounts.gist: Morris had bought a jug of whisky and took to the woods to enjoy it; no one of either color was harmed.

framing.detail: The Savannah Morning News headed the first report 'Evidence that Barnwell Negroes Have Murdered a White Man.'
The Sun ran it under 'Negroes and Whites Shooting Each Other in All Parts of the State,' warning that 'a war of races is threatened.'
The Sun and Tribune treated the ending as comedy ('He Only Had the Jim-Jams', 'A Race War That Fizzled Out'), using slurs while calling the hiding Black residents 'poor negroes'.
The Columbia wire called it a 'ridiculous ending' and stressed no damage to anyone.
The National Leader mocked the 'refined' white citizens who armed and turned out en masse.
A weekly news digest said the race war was 'inaugurated by the whites' of the county.

conflicts.note: The Charleston and Columbia dispatches written at the time place the finding on the 19th; the later weekly digest's '21st' is likely the date the wire ran.
